prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how import competition and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wages

statement.case_for: My ballot and my three names are unchanged. What changed is the scope of the citation. B038 combines newly assembled data, a transparent local-labour-market design and a finding that the field has absorbed: trade and technology shocks produce concentrated, lasting adjustment costs, not quick reallocation. It has more than a decade of replication, critique and extension behind it, so durability can actually be assessed. That matters for the maturity criterion, because the main alternative I take seriously, B002, has a shorter record and depends more on restricted data. The round 1 exchange showed me that the credit is clean only for the empirical core. Teorell, Friberg and Hjalmarsson all say a coherent prize should rest on the evidence about exposure and adjustment, not on the whole task framework, and the chair's summary shows nobody claims that framework wholesale for this trio. I accept that. I have therefore narrowed the citation to import competition and technological change as measured in local labour markets, and I no longer rely on the task view as a rationale. Dorn is retained over Katz because he is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers and of the Autor-Dorn work on job polarisation. Katz's wage-structure contribution is real but is a differently framed prize. I also drop the remark in my opening that B038 had broad placement among colleagues. That is a support count and says nothing about merit. My case rests on design, measurement, durability and attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that the entry combines two programmes with different lineages. The narrowed citation avoids claiming the task framework, but it also gives up some of the conceptual payoff that made the entry attractive. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects remain contested, and shift-share identification has been criticised. I read that as refinement of the conditions for valid inference, not a reversal of the core finding, but it is a real discount on the magnitudes. Proximity to the 2023, 2024 and 2025 prizes on labour-market history, institutions and technological change could reduce the Committee's appetite, though I think those awards concern different contributions. Finally, the attribution is defensible rather than unique. A Katz-centred wage-structure version would be a legitimate rival framing, and I cannot show that the Dorn version is uniquely correct.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B002 first and B038 only fifth. He agrees the China-shock work is the cleanly attributable core of B038 and says any B038 citation should be limited to that contribution. He keeps B038 below B002 because of the shift-share identification debate and the persistence question.
responses.response: I accept his scope condition and have written the citation accordingly. It names import competition and technological change as measured in local labour markets and does not claim the task framework. We still differ on the ranking. The identification debate is a reason to read the magnitudes cautiously, but the qualitative finding has been checked with different outcomes, pre-trends and other designs. The neighbourhood-effects work in B002 has had less time for that kind of independent testing, and Teorell himself concedes the restricted-data problem. Our shared criterion is measurement together with causal design. My view is that B038 currently has the longer record of passing it. I would not oppose B002 on merit if the Committee judged it mature enough.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B002 first and now includes Friedman. She treats the youth of the programme and restricted-data access as a real discount on maturity, and says she would not strongly oppose a mature candidate if the Committee puts maturity first.
responses.response: I value her candour that restricted data limits independent replication, because it is the main reason I place B002 behind B038 and not ahead of it. Where we differ is how much weight the multiple-design argument can bear. Cross-checks between the descriptive and the causal strands are useful, but they are not the same as independent teams working on open data. If B002 advances, I agree with her and with Teorell that Friedman is a better third name than Katz for a prize defined by population-data measurement. Katz is then better placed in the wage-structure framing on B038. I do not claim B038 is free of its own debates. Its design has been tested by more outside groups, which is why I weigh it first.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B038 seventh. He doubts that shift-share identification withstands current scrutiny, notes that the task framework owes much to scholars not listed, and says he would be more comfortable if the achievement were defined as the China-shock evidence alone.
responses.response: His request for a narrow definition has moved my citation, and I think it is the right discipline. On identification, I distinguish between the magnitudes and the finding. The methodological literature has tightened the conditions for valid shift-share inference, but results that rely on pre-trends, several outcome margins and designs other than a single instrument have held up as a pattern. I would not tell him the critique is trivial, and I accept that it lowers confidence in point estimates. One qualification to his China-shock-only framing: the Autor-Dorn polarisation work is a technology-exposure result that the same three authors produced, so I keep technological change in the citation but make no claim over the wider task lineage. If the Committee wanted trade alone, the same three names would still be the right ones.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B013 first and B038 fifth. He has moved toward Autor, Hanson and Dorn as the more defensible grouping if B038 advances, but is still concerned about overlap with the 2024 prize and about debate over the China-shock magnitudes. He also asks how theory with mixed empirical tests should be compared with empirical programmes with debated magnitudes.
responses.response: I appreciate that he has settled on Dorn, which removes one of the attribution disputes. On the 2024 overlap, I continue to read that prize as concerning long-run institutional determinants of prosperity, while B038 is about measured adjustment to specific shocks, so I treat the overlap as thematic. On his comparison question, I do not mark a candidate down for being theory. The mixed record of the Protection for Sale predictions is what lowers B013 for me, not its conceptual nature, and the debated magnitudes in B038 lower my confidence in point estimates without touching the qualitative finding. I would add that his B013 and B027 views overlap with my alternative B027, and I agree it is the least examined candidate on the shortlist. That is a reason for caution about my own second preference, not a reason to move it up.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats the trade-exposure and technology-exposure results as one contribution, and whether a citation that excludes the task framework is still compelling enough to carry the prize.
How far the shift-share identification critique and the long-run persistence debate should lower confidence in the China-shock magnitudes, as against the qualitative finding.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. My preference rests on authorship of the central empirical papers, and a differently framed wage-structure prize would reverse it.
Whether proximity to the 2023, 2024 and 2025 prizes on adjacent labour and technology topics should count against B038, and on what common standard.
Whether B002 will be judged mature enough to overtake B038 given the restricted-data constraint, and whether the third name there is Friedman or Katz.
My assessments rely on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, without independent verification of the empirical literature.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from my supplied profile. None of the credited names on B038, B002 or B027 appears among my listed co-authors or institutional ties. My research on electrification, railroads and labour outcomes has thematic proximity to technology and labour-market change, which is a field familiarity and not a personal connection, and I treat it as such. I share a Lund connection with Tommy Andersson and, formerly, Jan Teorell. That is a colleague tie and not a candidate tie, and I have engaged with Teorell's arguments on their merits. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
